title: Billing usage aggregation and cost analysis

opening.headline: This document covers the method of dividing invoice numbers by team and workload units.
body: The invoice for the month shows only the total and product-specific amounts, making it impossible to determine which team's specific work increased costs. Without knowing the cause, it is impossible to identify cost reduction opportunities or establish criteria for cost allocation.

In this class, we examine Databricks' billing system table structure and aggregation queries, as well as Snowflake's feature-level usage views, and walk through the process of narrowing down usage by date, product, team, and job to identify the root causes of usage spikes.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the billing usage system tables and cost aggregation.
Usage data can be broken down by team and workload unit.

screens.title: Cannot categorize invoice numbers by cause
screens.lead: After reading about the difficulties faced by the team that received the monthly invoice, consider why the total amount is insufficient based solely on the sum of numbers.

visual.alt: This shows the invoice total being broken down by team, product, and task unit.

paragraphs: The monthly invoice shows a total and itemized amounts by product. However, it does not indicate which team's workload increased costs this month solely based on the invoice. Even if the total has doubled since last month, you would still be uncertain about where to focus improvements.

If the cause is unknown, it's impossible to determine where to reduce or assign cost responsibilities. In such cases, each platform keeps billing data open in system tables or usage views. By directly querying this data, you can break down totals by date, product, team, and work unit.

In Databricks, account billable usage is accumulated record by record in the system.billing.usage table. In Snowflake, feature-specific Account Usage views display usage metrics such as tokens and credits.

This course explains the structure and aggregation methods of the billing usage table, and walks through the process of breaking down usage data by team and workload to identify the root causes of usage spikes.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Claim data is the original source for cost analysis. Dashboards or reports are summaries based on this original source, so root cause analysis must begin with the original data.

screens.title: Have you ever directly queried claim data?
screens.lead: Think about it yourself. You don't need to enter an answer; once you select a question, the instructor's summary will be displayed.

items.prompt: What columns are needed to segment by team and workload?
items.answer: The volume record should contain tags to distinguish teams and identifiers to distinguish workloads. In Databricks billing tables, custom_tags and usage_metadata serve this purpose. Tags are important not only because they have values but also because they actually exist—empty fields, even if present, cannot be parsed.

items.prompt: How can I verify that the totals are correct?
items.answer: Claim data may be subject to corrections and may arrive with delays, so the result of a sum can change depending on which records are included. When the claim number and query results do not match, the first place to suspect is how the correction records were handled.

items.prompt: How finely should aggregation units be divided?
items.answer: If it's too large, the cause is absorbed into the sum; if it's too small, it becomes noisy and makes it difficult to detect meaningful changes. A typical balance point is at the team and workload level. This balance is revisited toward the end of the class.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the columns that make up the Databricks billing table.

screens.title: Databricks Billing System Table Structure
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to verify which primary breakdown axis each key column in system.billing.usage represents.

data.caption: Key fields and usage of system.billing.usage
rows: usage_date, usage_start_time, usage_end_time
Date and start/end times of the used record
usage_date is a field intended to speed up date-based aggregations and is used with period conditions and daily trends.
sku_name
Billing item name. Example: STANDARD_ALL_PURPOSE_COMPUTE
It knows why the product increased.
usage_quantity, usage_unit
Quantity consumed and unit (e.g., DBU)
This is a consolidated item. Also check the usage_unit to ensure records with different units are not mixed into a single sum.
custom_tags
User-defined tag map attached to the usage record
Team, environment, and other organizational units are separated. Only existing tags in the record are used for parsing.
usage_metadata
job_id, cluster_id, warehouse_id, endpoint_name, etc. work and compute identifiers
It descends by workload. Some values are filled based on the compute type, while the rest are null.
identity_metadata
Entity information related to usage
Tracks who executed it.
billing_origin_product
The product that caused the issue. Example: JOBS
Grouped from a product perspective. One product can be charged against multiple SKUs.
record_type
One of ORIGINAL, RETRACTION, or RESTATEMENT
Indicates whether it has been corrected. If no correction has been made, it is ORIGINAL.
data.notes: This table aggregates usage across multiple regions into a single location, showing the total usage for an account. Records typically appear within 12 hours. This arrival timeframe applies only to records with record_type set to ORIGINAL. When corrections are made, either RETRACTION and RESTATEMENT records may be added, or only RETRACTION records may be added. A RETRACTION record has all values identical to the original record except that usage_quantity is negative, thereby offsetting the original value, while a RESTATEMENT record contains the corrected value. Therefore, when summing usage_quantity, the original value is removed and only the replacement value remains if a correction is applied; if only a cancellation (RETRACTION) is made, the usage quantity is offset. If only ORIGINAL records are selected for summation, corrections are not reflected, resulting in a discrepancy with the invoice.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the meaning of "heat," let's examine the actual aggregation queries line by line.

screens.title: Read aggregate queries by unit.
screens.lead: This is a query that breaks down usage over the past 7 days by date, team, and task. The description on the right explains the role assigned to each line and the symptoms that occur when the query is misused.

data.code:
SELECT usage_date,
       custom_tags['team'] AS team,
       usage_metadata.job_id AS job_id,
       usage_unit,
       SUM(usage_quantity) AS quantity
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_date >= date_sub(current_date(), 7)
GROUP BY ALL
HAVING quantity != 0
ORDER BY quantity DESC

notes.note: This sets the breakdown axis. Select date, team tag, work ID, and unit together. Removing an axis causes that dimension to be aggregated. Incorrectly specifying a tag key results in an empty team column and no breakdown, while removing a unit mixes different units within the same aggregate.

SUM(usage_quantity) is included in the aggregation. Due to aggregation, RETRACTION offsets the original value, and when RESTATEMENT occurs, the replacement value remains. Corrections are not reflected if rows are processed one at a time or if the maximum value is used.

Specify which table and which period to view. Since usage_date is a column used for fast date-based aggregation, it should be included in the period condition. Without a period condition, the query will scan the entire period slowly and weekly comparisons will not be possible. Records are typically reported within 12 hours, so today's values might still be incomplete.

GROUP BY ALL groups all selected columns, not the SUM. The HAVING quantity != 0 completely cancels out items that have become zero. If we use a WHERE record_type = 'ORIGINAL' filter instead, the corrections are not applied, leading to incorrect values.

Sorts by higher values first, placing the teams and tasks that are used most prominently at the top. In Snowflake, this is accomplished via account usage views by function. Views such as AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY, CORTEX_AGENT_USAGE_HISTORY, and CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY exist, each with different units—tokens, messages, provided time—and thus must be aligned and aggregated on the same axis.

screens.outro: Having completed the query reading, let's now work through an example of progressively narrowing down the root cause of the surge.

screens.title: A case study of identifying the root cause of sudden cost increases for specific workloads
screens.lead: The instructor will step-by-step walk through an example where this week's total is twice that of last week's. Click the following arrow to narrow the query one step at a time.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: This week's total is twice that of last week. Looking only at invoices, you cannot determine where the increase occurred. In such cases, you must progressively narrow down the scope—from a broad to a narrow focus—without descending into teams or specific tasks, to avoid missing intermediate clues.

steps.title: Step 1: Daily Totals
steps.body: SELECT usage_date, SUM(usage_quantity) FROM system.billing.usage grouped by usage_date to observe the daily trend. If a previously flat line starts rising from a specific date, that date has been narrowed down to the start of a spike. If the line rises gradually, it is more likely indicative of a change in usage patterns rather than a single event.

steps.title: Step 2: Divide by product
steps.body: After that date, add conditions and include sku_name in the GROUP BY. By reading which SKU quantities have increased, you narrow down the root cause to be either compute, serverless, or model serving.

steps.title: Step 3: Move down to the team and task level
steps.body: When custom_tags['team'] and usage_metadata.job_id are added, the result shows that a single job from a specific team accounts for most of the usage increase. If many rows have an empty team column, this signals that usage without tags cannot be attributed to any specific team. In such cases, the tagging rules should be reviewed and corrected first.

steps.title: Step 4: Root Cause Identification and Sharing
steps.body: Determine the root cause by comparing the change history of the task. For example, verify whether there were any changes during the same period, such as longer prompts or increased call frequency. Once confirmed, share the findings with the responsible team, including the relevant query. For Snowflake, follow the same flow by narrowing down using REQUEST_ID or user ID in the feature-specific usage view.

steps.title: Summary: Reason for the narrowing order
steps.body: The reason we start with date is to identify when the surge occurred, so that we can compare it against the change history. We look at the product afterward because the responsibilities differ across areas such as compute, hosting, and storage. The team and tasks are defined at the end to assign accountability and actions. If we descend through all dimensions at once, there will be too many rows, making patterns difficult to identify.

screens.outro: To repeatedly investigate causes, aggregation units and outlier detection thresholds must be defined.

screens.title: Define anomaly detection and aggregation units
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the aggregation unit. When the unit changes, observe what appears and what is hidden.

stops.body: This is the widest unit. While the overall totals' changes are visible, the causes remain obscured. The surge in one team can offset a decline in another, making the total appear flat. It is appropriate for verifying aggregate figures, such as in a budget report, but insufficient for root cause analysis.

We check what type of consumption has increased. While the response direction is determined based on whether it's compute or model serving, we do not know who specifically caused the increase. It is appropriate to break down the issue at the stage before assigning responsibility.

This is a unit that includes team tags and task identifiers. Since both the cause and responsible team are revealed together, it generally leads to effective actions and serves as a balance point. To use this unit, tag rules must first be established, and the amount of unused tags should be minimal.

This is the finest granularity unit. It is accurate but generates a large number of records, leading to high noise levels and a tendency to misinterpret temporary fluctuations as anomalies. Individual records are used only after a root cause has been established and validated; they are not suitable for routine anomaly detection.

Anomaly detection works by comparing daily usage against the average of the previous few days and highlighting days that significantly deviate. Considering correction records and delayed arrivals, the most recent few days should be treated as provisional. Therefore, responsibility is not assigned based solely on today's value, but only after the values have stabilized.

Team-level breakdowns only hold under the assumption that tags are present. If a significant portion of usage lacks tags, the team-level numbers only partially explain the actual usage. Therefore, determining the aggregation unit is not merely a query design decision—it is also an operational rule that establishes and enforces tagging policies. Tracking the ratio of tagless usage as a separate metric allows you to verify whether the tagging rules are being followed, and as this ratio decreases, the reliability of team-level breakdowns increases. Setting a target ratio further improves this approach.

screens.outro: I will now summarize the content of the lecture.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: We organize the flow of breaking down request data by cause. While reading, compare it with our organization's aggregation methodology.

paragraphs: Billing data is the source for cost analysis. To determine root causes, analysis must start from the record-level usage table, not the total sum of the invoice.

Databricks' system.billing.usage can be broken down by product, team, and job units using sku_name, custom_tags, and usage_metadata. When aggregating, usage_quantity values are summed up with proper records being offset, and only ORIGINAL records are not selected.

Snowflake provides account usage views by feature, showing tokens and credits, with each view using different units that must be aligned on the same axis for aggregation. You can also calculate total operational costs by query, warehouse, and user identifier.

The root cause is narrowed down in the order of date, product, team, and workflow sequence. If a tag is empty, it cannot be decomposed, and the recent values from the past few days may change due to corrections and delayed arrivals, so they are considered provisional.

Going back to the introductory example, the reason the total doubled was because we had to look for usage records instead of invoices. Once you become familiar with the process—setting the time point by date, identifying the product type, and assigning responsibility by team and task—the next spike becomes much easier to explain. By storing this sequence as a query set, anyone can analyze it in the same way.

callout.label: inspection questions
callout.text: What is our aggregation unit, and can we identify the cause of cost increases and the responsible team using that unit?

checks.q:
The query results do not match the invoice. What is the most plausible cause?  

SELECT usage_date, SUM(usage_quantity)  
FROM system.billing.usage  
WHERE record_type = 'ORIGINAL'  
GROUP BY usage_date
options: On the day of correction, if cancellation or re-entry operations are not performed, the value before correction remains.
usage_date is a column that cannot be used as an aggregation axis.
Use COUNT instead of SUM to have DBU aggregated
Usage across multiple regions is not included in this table.
checks.explain: Correction combines the cancellation of negative values and, if present, the re-entry operation, reflecting these changes. If only ORIGINAL is filtered, these operations are omitted, leaving the value prior to correction.

wrong.1: usage_date is a column intended for quickly performing date-based aggregations.
wrong.2: Aggregation uses SUM, while COUNT counts the number of rows.
wrong.3: This table displays the total account usage across multiple regions in one place.

checks.intro: Review the reasons for queries that do not match the invoice. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, the corrected record was filtered, which caused the discrepancy.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Other options are misunderstandings regarding the use of temperature or summation functions. Recall again how corrections are represented as records.

checks.q: Let's consider the order of narrowing down the reasons why weekly costs have doubled.
items: Find the start date of the surge by aggregating by usage_date
On that date, separate by sku_name and find the products that appear repeatedly.
Searches for specific teams or jobs by custom_tags and job_id
Determines the cause by comparing the change history of the task against it.
checks.explain: Narrows from a wide axis to a narrow axis in the order of date → product → team/work, and finalizes it through change history.
checks.intro: Consider the order for narrowing down the causes of the surge. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. It goes from a wide axis to a narrow axis.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Consider which step—date, product, team and task, or confirmed—serves as a prerequisite for the next step.

checks.q: If there are many usage entries with empty custom_tags in the team-based cost breakdown?
options: Calculate the average and distribute it evenly among the team.
Just looking at the SKU sum is sufficient.
Since it cannot be decomposed, the tag rules must be established first.
Recently, finalizes the value over a few days and assigns responsibility.
checks.explain: There is no basis for dividing by team if no tag is present. Additionally, due to correction records and delayed arrivals, the situation has been treated as provisional for the past few days.

wrong.1: The total SKU count alone is insufficient to determine which team increased their inventory.
wrong.3: In recent days, it is being treated provisionally due to corrections and delayed arrivals.

checks.intro: Select a response for when there are many empty tags in usage. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The premise of parsing is tag rules.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfounded allocations or the finalization of provisional values incorrectly distribute responsibilities. First, verify whether the required heat for decomposition is adequately supplied.

glossary.def: This is the system.billing.usage table from Databricks, which records accountable usage by record unit.
This is a query operation that aggregates usage records by period, SKU, tag, and other dimensions.
This is a method of dividing the total by execution units such as tasks or apps to identify the cause.
Used with the user-defined tag map attached to the usage record, it is employed for team-level breakdowns.
A value indicating whether the volume record is the original or has been corrected (canceled or reentered).

misconceptions.myth: Just looking at the invoice total is sufficient for cost management.
misconceptions.fact: Root cause analysis requires decomposition of SKU, tags, and work units.

misconceptions.myth: If tags are applied later, past usage is also broken down by team.
misconceptions.fact: The tags already present in the usage records are used only for decomposition. Tag rules must be established first.

misconceptions.myth: The most recent several-day values are definitive.
misconceptions.fact: Due to possible arrival delays and corrections in the recent days, this is considered a provisional figure.

misconceptions.myth: Only include rows where record_type is ORIGINAL to achieve greater accuracy.
misconceptions.fact: Correction includes both cancellation operations and, if present, reassignment operations. The total must be summed to yield the correct value.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The claim data is the original source for cost analysis.
system.billing.usage can be broken down by SKU, tag, and operation ID.
Snowflake provides tokens and credits via feature-based usage views.
The root cause is narrowed down by date, product, team, and task order.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Our organization aggregates billing data at what unit, and can we identify the cause of the surge based on that unit?
